utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Prosecution is still cross-examining. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Di Fazio: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Blagojevic, I'll be mercifully brief this afternoon, so you won't be kept for too much longer. I just need to clarify a matter that arises from yesterday's transcript. An answer that you gave was inaudible, and I'd just like it to be made clear for the purposes of the transcript. You recall yesterday I was asking you about the possibility of Croats or Muslims who were intending to leave simply coming to you, or the department of housing, and informing you or the department of housing that they were going to leave, and so the process of recording their property and furniture could take place or could occur in a fairly calm and unhurried and indeed more thorough way. And you answered that question, and I think it was with the answer yes, but in the transcript it's inaudible. So I put the question to you again. Would that have been sensible and possible? Could Croats and Muslims have come to you and said, "We're going do leave. Let's get the inventory of furniture and so on done now, rather than leaving it to chance"?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they would come, but it was quite rarely. Much more frequently they would leave the keys to their property with their relations or with their friends.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you find that puzzling, given that you have said that the population knew that there was this process of acquiring abandoned houses for the use of refugees? Do you find it strange that people didn't come to you, given that that was widespread knowledge, and endeavour to do it in a more -- in this more calm and unhurried way? It would make sense, after all, wouldn't it, for someone who is going to leave to come to you and say, "Look, I'm going to abandon my property. Please make sure that it's all accorded properly and done according to the systems that you have spoken of"?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why people didn't come, but they had occasion to come. They had the opportunity to come.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Yesterday afternoon you also testified that occasionally you held lists of exchanges, people who had been exchanged, in your hands, and you said that you occasionally had these lists. And I was then asking you about the practicality of using the exchange lists to find out who -- to find out where abandoned houses might be located. My question is: How did you get hold of these lists?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I got them from the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Tadic facilitate the provision of these lists to you?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I got the lists from Mr. Tadic. MR. DI FAZIO: Would Your Honours just bear with me for one moment, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic was involved in the Red Cross in Bosanski Samac, he was working with them, was he not?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you go to the Red Cross and get a hold of the lists precisely so that you could find out who had been exchanged and whose homes would be empty?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would occasionally receive these lists, but these lists were not suitable for our use -- to be used for our purposes, because we did not know exactly whether the complete family had been exchanged or just members of the family in question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Okay. Okay. It's on page 2, line 23. Answer: "I believe that I got them from the Red Cross." That's a very, so to say, "I believe." Did he get them or did he not get them? MR. DI FAZIO: I was going to go into that topic right now, if Your Honour pleases. Perhaps if you allow me to deal with that topic and then if anything arises from that, perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, first of all, the way your answer came across, "I believe I got them from the Red Cross" imports a degree of uncertainty. Simple question: Did you or did you not get exchange lists from the Red Cross? That's the first thing I want to know.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From this time distance, I cannot exactly recall from whom I got these lists.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You may not know from whom personally you got the lists, but did you get the lists from someone, whoever it may be, in the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose yes, this is what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was your purpose in obtaining these lists? For what reason did you get them?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We used these lists as auxiliary material for the purpose of allocating our living space to refugees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That was one method for ascertaining, finding out about abandoned homes, wasn't it, but there were other methods that you used; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Just the way the answer was translated, it's not entirely clear to me. You agree that you used other methods for discovering, finding, abandoned homes?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Prosecutor. Isn't that question answered already by information from the neighbours and other sources? Is it necessary to ask the same questions once again? MR. DI FAZIO: Well, if I'm repeating myself, it certainly is not necessary, and I apologise if I am repeating myself. But I just wanted to make sure that we knew every single method that abandoned homes were found for refugees. That's all I wanted to clarify. And I can be very brief with it, with this issue, if I can just pursue it briefly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just wrap this topic up for us, if you can, Witness. The methods of discovering abandoned homes, were they the exchange lists, reports from neighbours, anything else that you can think of?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Also our inspection of the situation in situ, which I also referred to yesterday, was another source.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. During the course of yesterday's evidence, Judge Williams asked you about abandoned property, and you were asked if you had to be shown some type of intention or some sort of intention not to return after 30 days, and you said that you had no information about that. Wouldn't the intention to return be absolutely crucial to determining whether or not a house had been abandoned that is, to ascertain whether it's truly been abandoned?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 30-day period was the period that we respected according to the decree.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I know about that. I've seen that in the decree, and I understand that's the definition of abandoned. The problem is, how do you know when 30 days have elapsed? You might go to a house, find it empty. Did you then wait 30 days from that point or did you declare it to be abandoned there and then?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we did was taking account or rather bearing in mind the information that we had collected on abandoned property on the basis of reports from the neighbours, on the basis of data collected by our own inspection on the spot, we could conclude what property had indeed been abandoned. But in the case that the owners or the possessors of the property in question returned, after the 30 days had elapsed, we would return such property and such housing and living space to their original owners and accommodate the refugees in question elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time that you were working in Bosanski Samac after September, did you ever see bus loads of Muslims and Croats being driven out of town on their way to exchanges in other parts of the country?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that such a phenomenon was taking place?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That would have been an ideal place to go to, wouldn't it, and ask the people on the buses: "What are your plans? Do you intend to return in the next 30 days or in the next two months, next six months," whatever?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. This is a really a very speculative question, so it's -- maybe my learned friend can be more precise with regard to the personal knowledge of this witness and his action, possible actions with regard to the issue. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm not asking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. The question is all right. The witness can answer. There's nothing calling for speculation. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question simply is: Going to the people on the buses as they're about to be bussed out on their way to these exchange points, that would have been an ideal method for ascertaining what their intentions were regarding abandonment of their homes?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It might have been an ideal method, but not one that I applied.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And my last question -- sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Could we find out why you didn't? Why was that not a method that you applied, being that you said you knew that the exchanges were taking place, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The decree on accommodation made no provision whatsoever, nor gave us any instructions to that effect, and simply we did not apply such a method. In view of the fact that the ongoing war operations were such that we had to work around the clock, literally, in order to accommodate the needy people or to repair the facilities for that purpose, and we did not avail ourselves, nor had the time to employ any other methods of data collection. Ours was a very busy service, and we worked very hard, and sometimes we did not even have enough paper and office supplies, nor did we have the necessary photocopiers or electricity in order to properly work, so that we actually operated under very difficult and special, extraordinary circumstances, addressing these very difficult matters. What I do know is that we did our work very professionally and very correctly, and how else can we explain that in our police and the army there were Muslims and Croats, that in the business sector, in the health sector, there were also experts of that ethnicity who remained in the territory of Samac municipality throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Just one small follow-up question. If I understand you, therefore, correctly, you only followed the decree and the instructions in the decree. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you. And last question: Could you remind me -- you may be mentioned this yesterday, but I don't have the transcript in front of me. Did the decree authorise you to go and talk to the neighbours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The answer that you gave to Her Honour's first question puzzles me. You say that the decree on accommodation made no provision whatsoever, but the decree specifically and repeatedly talks about abandonment, the idea or notion of abandonment. When you're talking about people's homes, it's really important, isn't it, to make sure that you've got guidelines or rules or regulations, to make absolutely sure they've abandoned their home? Wouldn't you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not fully understand your question, but I agree with the last part of your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you then gave a lengthy -- the second part of your answer was lengthy and dealt with the difficult wartime conditions. I accept entirely what you say, that there were wartime conditions and things were very difficult for everyone. However, I fail to see the difficulty involved in simply asking people on the bus what their plans were, and indeed if you weren't going to do it at that point, perhaps you could have gone to Mr. Tadic and asked him to get a statement or a little document, or at least an interview, a simple question, anything at all to ascertain what the intentions of these people were regarding abandonment. In other words, given the hard conditions, the hard wartime conditions, something could have been done, couldn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps something could have been done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday Judge Lindholm asked you a question regarding why there were abandoned houses and apartments, and you gave an answer, in which you said that many people had a chance to leave the town and the municipality, and you said it wasn't just Croats and Muslims, but it was also Serbs. Do you remember giving that evidence?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall seeing or hearing of any Serbs leaving the town through the exchange process and put on a bus with their suitcase and taken off to an exchange point somewhere?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of Serbs having been exchanged. However, neither did Croats or Muslims go there through such exchanges. Mostly this took place via Yugoslavia, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's been in this case, Mr. Blagojevic, uncontradicted evidence, a large body of uncontradicted evidence, that large numbers of Muslims and Croats left the municipality and the town of Bosanski Samac via the system of exchanges, which manifested itself by being placed on buses and taken off to various exchange points, sometimes in Bosnia and sometimes in Croatia. Are you aware of that phenomenon?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Samac municipality, the Muslims lived just in town, and I believe that I've already said that I knew that exchanges were taking place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Okay. My question is very simple: Did you hear of or ever see Serbs leaving the municipality of Bosanski Samac or the town of Bosanski Samac via this same system of exchanges: Being exchanged and put on a bus and taken off to the exchange point?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Serbs were not exchanged in that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me turn to just one -- to another topic. You gave some evidence yesterday of -- towards the end of your evidence of contact that you had with Dr. Blagoje Simic, and as I read your evidence, you seem to be saying that you had a number of business meetings with Mr. Blagoje Simic. That's correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, business meetings, to do with the work of the secretariat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. And was this not only taking place after the beginning of 1993, when the Municipal Assembly was up and running, but also before that, that is, between September and early 1993, when the War Presidency was in existence? Did you have meetings when the War Presidency was running?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had meetings before the assembly started working.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you had a chance to see who was on the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the War Presidency did not meet in full composition at all times, and I know that President Blagoje was a member of the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Okay. Let me put some other names to you and see if you can tell us if they're on the War Presidency. What about Mr. Bozo Ninkovic? Was he on the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think he was, no. I think that he attended the meetings of the War Presidency from time to time by virtue of office, because he was in fact the secretary of the department of the Ministry of Defence at republican level, and so by virtue of office, he attended the meetings. That's my opinion, anyway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Would Your Honours just bear with me for one minute, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Mr. Simeon Simic and Mr. Mirko Lukic? Were they on War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that Mr. Simeon Simic was, as for Mirko Lukic, I really don't know, because when I arrived in the municipality, he was the deputy president of the Executive Board, and by virtue of office, I don't think that meant that he was a member of the War Presidency. He didn't automatically belong there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Milan Simic and Stevan Todorovic? Were they on the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume Milan Simic was, yes. As for Mr. Todorovic, following on the same logics as Mr. Bozo Ninkovic, I would assume that -- and he was the chief of the public security station, so it was a republican organ and not a municipal organ. So he was head of a republican organ and not a municipal body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. So that's one of the tests for determining whether someone was on the War Presidency, namely, whether their job was in a republican organ or whether it was in a municipal organ; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's my opinion. That's what I think, anyway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You also described briefly yesterday Zasavica, and in your evidence you said that the people in Zasavica were happy. You said that it was a nice, wealthy village, and you said that it was a nice, pleasant place in which to live. Are you talking about after September of 1992, when you took up your duties?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And presumably you can speak from first-hand knowledge because you presumably went along to Zasavica and were able to see what the situation was, particularly as Serbs from a village -- I won't venture to pronounce it. I'm sorry. I can't recall it. Something like Gasovici [phoen]. Particularly because Serbs being housed there. That's your evidence, is it not?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Zasavica there were also Serbs who had been put up there, yes, accommodated in Zasavica, but they came from the village of Gostovic. I think that's what I was talking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Thank you for clarifying that.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The environs of Zasavica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for clarifying that. But what I'm primarily interested in is this: Your description of Zasavica as a place where the people were happy, a nice, wealthy village and a nice, pleasant place to live, that's based on first-hand experience; you went there and you saw the place, I take it.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Excuse me. Would Your Honours just bear with me again for one moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Mr. Bozo Ninkovic?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He gave evidence in this case, and he described Zasavica, and he said that it --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no problem with this, but there was a principle here not to put testimony of one witness to another. MR. DI FAZIO: I can approach it differently. I won't put the direct testimony, if you wish, but I want to put the concept, the idea of what the witness said. I'm quite happy to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I think we've been going by that rule, don't confront witnesses -- MR. DI FAZIO: With direct testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Except for the accused. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me put it to you this way: Did you ever see anything in Zasavica that tended to indicate to you that people had been isolated there, separated from the rest of the population, guards, confinement to the village and by that - I'll be clear - of the non-Serb population?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the village of Zasavica, I did visit the village, yes, and at the entrance to the village, there was the police there. The police did not have the task of prohibiting anybody from leaving, either Serbs or Croats. What those people were doing there, what their job was, was to ensure that unauthorised people, somebody who would, for example, take Croatian property, movable property, and take it off, to see that that didn't happen. So this was a sort of safety barrier. And I mentioned one man, a man named Ivica, and I cooperated with him extremely well. I think his surname was Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But you understood the police at the entrance to the village to be protecting the Croats, protecting them, and the Serbs, presumably, and protecting Croat and Serbian property, and that's all that they were doing; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you very much, Mr. Blagojevic. I have no other questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Re-examination, Mr. Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should just like to ask the Trial Chamber for an interpretation before I go and cross-examine. I'm interested in hearing your position. When one Defence team did not ask a single question in the examination-in-chief and through the cross-examination, subjects crop up which are essential for that Defence team. May that Defence team go back and ask certain questions in the re-examination that it did not ask? We haven't had a situation of that kind arise so far, so perhaps the Trial Chamber could give me guidance and the Defence team for Mr. Miroslav Tadic might like to ask a few questions about what we've just heard. But I'd like to hear the position of the Trial Chamber in this regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The Trial Chamber will allow the other parties to ask questions of the witness, but they must do it before the re-examination. Mr. Pantelic, you first wait, because you are re-examining, so you will do it last. Re-examined by Mr. Krgovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My name is Dragan Krgovic. I'm one of the Defence attorneys for Mr. Miroslav Tadic, and I shall be asking you a few questions connected to the questions asked by the Prosecutor, that is to say, they have to do with the actions and conduct of Mr. Miroslav Tadic. The Prosecutor asked you the following: Do you know that -- or did you know that the Croats and Muslims left in buses, left Samac in buses and went to other areas of Bosnia and also to Croatia? And your answer was affirmative. You said you did know about that.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me now, please: Were there any Serbs in this procedure, any Serbs that expressed the desire, if you yourself know about this, to go to enemy territory, that is to say, territory under the control of Muslims and Croats? MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, unless my recollection serves me wrongly, I asked that indeed twice, and the answer unequivocal: No. What's there to clarify? He was quite clear about that, and I belaboured the topic a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My line of question, Your Honour, is just where the Serbs went, to which territories, and whether there were any instances, any cases of the Serbs being exchanged, or rather the Serbs wishing to be exchanged. My question is, in fact: Did they wish to be exchanged and go to other territories? MR. DI FAZIO: Very well. I'll withdraw my objection if the question is framed in that manner, if they expressed a wish to be exchanged. We know that none were exchanged, because the witness has made that clear. But now we have to find out if they wanted to be exchanged, and to that I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you happen to know if any Serbs wished to go to territories under the control of the Muslims and Croats, for example, bearing in mind the fact that there was a war on between the Serbs, on one side, and the Muslims on the other?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think that there were any Serbs who expressed the wish to be exchanged and go to territory under the control of Croats and Muslims, completely under their control. Quite the contrary; a large number of people came in on exchange basis from the territories that were under the control of the Croats and Serbs. So a large number of Serbs came in from those territories.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you happen to know whether any evacuations of Serbs in buses was organised from Bosanski Samac, and also other ethnic groups, taking them in the direction of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the very beginning of the war, there were several buses, several bus loads of people that left in the direction of Bijeljina and further on into Serbia and there were Serbs in the buses, as well as Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As your -- well, that completes my examination. Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The other team? No. Mr. Pantelic, re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Re-examined by Mr. Pantelic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you were asked by the Prosecutor about something, although it is outside the frameworks of the indictment in terms of time, but he asked you something with respect to your membership, your later membership in the SDS party, and you gave him your answer, and that isn't being challenged at all. But in that regard, I should like to say that he also asked you whether or not the SDS party in 1992 or 1993 had any results and that that's why you joined the party later on. Now, do you happen to know whether political parties were banned from working in 1992 and 1993? MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, none of this arises from my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The membership -- MR. DI FAZIO: The membership it, the membership did, the membership did. That's clear, and I've got no problem with that if he wants to ask questions regarding membership but you also recall the witness said he had an opportunity to see the policies of the SDS at work for the preceding two years and he was content with that and accepted -- and that was one of the reasons why he joined the SDS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The question of political parties being banned didn't arise. MR. DI FAZIO: That didn't arise, so I don't see how that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic. MR. DI FAZIO: How that arises, unless that's got something to do with his joining the SDS. But I can't see what the connection is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I will clarify that. We should not waste the time. Your Honour, yesterday the question of my learned friend from Prosecution was the following: And by that time you had seen its policies, related to SDS, its policies, at work in Bosanski Samac for a period of almost two years or thereabouts; would that be right? And the answer was "yes." So it's very much related to the question raised by the Prosecution, and I'm going to explore that issue. That was his question. That was the Prosecution's question. It was just at the beginning of yesterday's cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Except that it's not clear what the work was. You can go ahead, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what I'm asking you, Mr. Blagojevic, is this, because you gave an affirmative answer to the question posed to you by the Prosecutor, and I quoted the question that was asked yesterday, I'm asking you now: Do you know, can you tell us something about whether the party functioned in 1992 and 1993 or not?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't say anything about the ban and how long the ban was in force for, but when I became a member and when -- at that time political activities were allowed, and there were other parties which set up their municipal boards as well, and they dealt with political issues and politics in general.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're talking about 1992 and 1993. Do you know that the work of the SDS party was frozen at the time?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for a certain period of time their work was frozen, yes, put on ice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the next question that the Prosecutor asked you was -- had to do with form, and it was linked to the so-called paramilitary units. As you are a well-educated man and you were a reserve officer as well, tell us, please, which of these two concepts is more acceptable and corresponds to the situation in the Samac territory better within the frameworks of military structures and formations, which notion, the notion of paramilitary units or volunteer units? Answer me that, please.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the conditions that prevailed in our region, I would say that the concept of volunteers, volunteer units, is a more acceptable term and concept.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next question that the Prosecutor asked you had to do with the renaming of the 17th Tactical Group, which came to be known as the 2nd Bosnian Brigade, Posavina Brigade, sorry. Do you happen to know when the members of the JNA, the JNA units, when they left the Samac region, or rather, Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was sometime in March -- May 1992. May 1992, according to a decision taken by the army of Yugoslavia and the condition was -- or rather, what led to this decision was a resolution on the part of the United Nations or something similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, just a moment. I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Everything is correct in the transcript. My friend just made a notification.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My next question has to do with that. Did any of the JNA officers from the 17th Tactical Group stay on, remain, being a native of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Did he remain in the 2nd Posavina Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the JNA left Samac, left the Samac municipality, no officers, no JNA officers who were not originally from Samac, remained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My next question: What were the origins of the soldiers that made up the 2nd Posavina Brigade after that brigade was set up? Where did these soldiers come from? Where did the men come from?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The men came from Samac and the surrounding villages. They were natives of that area, from Pelagicevo and the surrounding villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next question that the Prosecutor asked you was this, probably not intentionally, but it's up to us to clarify the point, and it has to do with the decision of the War Presidency about disposing with abandoned property. And in his questions, he asked you, quite directly, whether the decision was made by Blagoje Simic, and you answered in the affirmative. Now I'm asking you this: Did Blagoje Simic make the decision personally or was the decision made by an institution of some kind, and if so, tell me which. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, unless I've forgotten the evidence, my memory is that I put to the witness that his appointment was made by Blagoje Simic because you've got Blagoje Simic's signature on the document. That's what I was -- that's what I think I put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yell. MR. DI FAZIO: And if Mr. Pantelic wants to ask something about that, I've got no objection, but it was his appointment, not disposal of -- sorry, not abandoned property that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. Maybe it's my mistake. I will rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a question of your appointment. Did he do so personally, on the basis of friendship or anything like that, Blagoje Simic, as a personage, did he appoint you or did your appointment come from some institution? What I'm asking you is: Who actually appointed you?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The signature on the appointment document is Blagoje Simic's, but above that it says "The president of the War Presidency," or something to that effect. So therefore, it is an institution, in actual fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did -- was Blagoje Simic in person in that institution? Did he constitute the institution was or it an institution with collective membership?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was a body, a collective body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday the Prosecutor went on to ask you this, and the question was -- had several parts to it. Your answer was yes, so this left some things unclear. What he asked you was this: "Is your evidence [In English] that a number of houses used for the accommodating refugees had been emptied as a result of the exchange process and detention process?" [Interpretation] And your answer was: "Yes, it is." So as you have already testified, and as you answered a previous question by the Prosecutor to the effect that you knew about exchanges but then you said that you did not know whether the abandoned property belonged to persons who were detainees, and this question incorporates both parts, I have to clear that point up with you. So what I'm asking you now is this: Were there instances in which you, as the secretariat for housing affairs, disposed of the apartments and homes of people who had been detained while they were in detention? So give us a brief answer to that first, please.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we did not dispose of the property of persons who were in detention. MR. DI FAZIO: Is the word -- I'm not trying to stop my friend from re-examining on this, but is the word "dispose" being used in the sense of making use of abandoned premises? Is that what Mr. Pantelic is ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also mentioned yesterday in your answers the town of Zenica, and you mentioned a female colleague of yours with whom you exchanged experiences about the situation of abandoned property over there. I don't think that is challenged, but just tell us for purposes of the record where Zenica is located and who Zenica belongs to.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zenica is in the central part of Bosnia and belongs to the Muslim and Croatian Federation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your responses to questions from the Prosecutor with respect to the lists of people going for the exchanges, I would like to ask you whether you know whether those lists were in the Executive Board. Did you receive information of that kind from the Executive Board as to the persons to be exchanged, the lists of persons to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I got them from the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A moment ago, asked by my learned colleague, you said that there were Serbs and other ethnic groups who left Samac. I would like to ask you the following: Are you aware of the fact -- do you know about the period from May to June, that Serbs, Muslims, and Croats left Samac and started off towards Yugoslavia, towards Belgrade, in fact, in buses? Do you know of that particular case? MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I object to that question. It's leading in the extreme, and Mr. Pantelic is cross-examining his own -- well, yes, in effect, cross-examining his own witness. The answer has been fairly squarely placed in the witness's mouth. Do you know from May to June that Serbs, Muslims and Croats left Samac? Now, the witness did say at the beginning of the outbreak of hostilities, at the beginning of outbreak of hostilities, Serbs, Muslims and Croats left. Yes, he did say that. And I've got no problem with Mr. Pantelic clarifying what the witness means when he said that. That's the proper scope of re-examination. But Mr. Pantelic isn't doing that. He's giving the answer to the witness. He's telling him, and that is what I object to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. It's absolutely founded objection. Because I was relating to the previous answer that his personal knowledge was that at the beginning of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Of the hostilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Conflict all three ethnicities left Samac. So that was the reason for me to clarify. Anyhow, I will rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Blagojevic, will you tell me, please, in connection with your previous answer, tell me: How did you come to learn that all three ethnic groups were leaving Samac when the war started? What is the source of your knowledge? And also tell us if you know where they were going.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that on the basis of conversations I had with friends whose family members or friends or relatives left to go to Yugoslavia, and those people were in touch with people in Yugoslavia. They stayed with them, they lived with them. So over a certain period of time, it was easy to learn where people were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And through those conversations, did you have occasion to learn what the motives of those people belonging to that ethnic group was to leave the territory of Samac?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason was the difficult situation and the war, which affected everyone equally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And my last question in this re-examination is the following: If you know, please tell us how Serb refugees arrived in Samac, using which means of transport or what kind of procedure, as you had contact with a certain number of refugees? Of course, if you know.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbs came to Samac in various ways. The vast majority of them came having been expelled, and these were mostly inhabitants of entire villages. I mentioned the village of Cernica, the village of Gostovic, Ljeskovica, Bistrovica, Zavidovici. They also came through the exchange process, and Serbs came whatever way they found to come, through friendly connections, crossing the defence lines which were held by Croats and Muslims, on the one side, and by the Serbs on the other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Blagojevic, but I think you omitted to answer a part of my question that related to the means of transport. What kind of means of transport did they use to come?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Towards the end of the war, I know that they came in trains and convoys of buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question is in 1992 and 1993.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly how they came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Blagojevic, for giving evidence. You are now finished and you may leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence counsel of Miroslav Tadic is ready to begin its Defence case, and at the beginning I shall avail myself of the right, on behalf of Miroslav Tadic's Defence, to make an opening statement. I have already given a copy of the opening statement to the interpreters, in my own language, and I think it will not take more than one hour. The first witness has already arrived and we've already served the list of witnesses to the registry, which we will abide by, I hope, at least with respect to the first few witnesses. Your Honours, my learned friends from the Prosecution, the first indictment against Miroslav Tadic was issued in July 1995. My client gave his first interview by telephone to the Prosecution on his own initiative in April 1996. He voluntarily surrendered to this Tribunal on the 14th of February, 1998, and of his own free will he agreed to be interviewed by the Prosecution over a period of two days. I'm beginning my opening statement by highlighting these facts in order to draw attention immediately to the fact that Miroslav Tadic has been waiting a long time for this moment, the moment when, by presenting his arguments, facts, and finally the truth, he will be able to disprove all the allegations against him ever since the first indictment to this moment when the Prosecution has rested its case. This Trial Chamber, over a period of almost one year of the presentation of evidence by the Prosecution, has heard the Prosecution's allegations and evidence, and also during the cross-examination has been able to hear the submissions of the Defence with respect to some of the statements of witnesses. This Trial Chamber has surely devoted due attention to the contents of the interviews of Miroslav Tadic with the Prosecution. In view of these circumstances, as well as the fact that prior to this opening statement some evidence has already been presented in the Defence case of Mr. Blagoje Simic, though I cannot say that it has been completed, we are aware of the fact that on the basis of all that has been presented so far, this Trial Chamber is aware to a considerable extent of the Defence case of Miroslav Tadic. The Defence, in its opening statement, will seek to focus your attention on a number of concepts which will be constantly repeated in the course of the presentation of evidence in this case. However, we have no intention, nor can we define and elaborate on those concepts. We will leave that to the Defence case itself. Our wish is to give an overview of some key institutions and concepts and to place them in the context of time and space, and thereby also to identify the role of Miroslav Tadic in all of that. I feel that our professional and even personal experience had very little to do with terms such as exchanges, civil defence or evacuation, to name a few. Therefore, in the course of the preparations for this case, it was rather complicated for us to grasp all this and to determine the place and role of our client in all of that. If I succeed in this opening statement to convey a part of what we ourselves have learnt, I'm quite confident that the Trial Chamber will have a clear and complete understanding of the testimony of witnesses and the written documents presented during the Defence case. According to the instructions of this Trial Chamber, Miroslav Tadic's Defence counsel will have 70 hours in which to examine witnesses and present its evidence. Our concept has been designed in such a way that through viva voce witnesses we wish to explain the most important aspects of work related to exchanges and civil defence, two components which are not linked amongst themselves but to which Miroslav Tadic -- in which Miroslav Tadic was involved throughout the indictment period. Some witnesses that the Defence has proposed should be heard as 92 bis statements will also describe from their standpoint certain broader aspects of life in Samac, and more specifically, the procedure of exchange, cooperation with the commission for exchange, with the local Red Cross, work duty, and the way in which these people experienced this work duty, and other concepts which were presented from one angle in the Prosecution case and which we now wish to throw light on from another angle. It is also our intention to describe life in the Samac municipality in the relevant period through the viva voce testimony of non-Serb citizens who stayed in Samac throughout the war. You will hear about the contacts they had with Tadic related to their day to day problems and particularly related to exchanges. Finally, reference will also be made to certain aspects of life in Samac which were not at all covered by the Prosecution in their case but which the Defence of Miroslav Tadic considers to be important for its case. The third group of witnesses proposed by the Defence counsel, through depositions, are again related to individual episodes linked to the incidents we heard about in the Prosecution case, but also there will be short statements regarding what these witnesses knew about certain problems of life in the municipalities of Samac and Odzak in the indictment period. The Defence is prepared to offer the Trial Chamber a large number of written documents about all the events relevant for Tadic's Defence, as well as some video recordings and photographs which we wish to complement all the evidence that will be presented before this Trial Chamber. I should now like to go into some greater detail into the main positions and submissions of the Defence and the manner in which we seek to prove them. Before I move on to specific submissions which we will seek to prove in our case, I wish to observe that the specifics of a joint trial, such as the Samac trial, necessarily leads to certain technical links between individual defences regarding the facts which are important for all the Defence teams. You were probably able to see for yourself that during the Defence case of Dr. Simic that certain elements of our own case were presented through the case of Dr. Simic, and I have in mind both the witness's testimony and the exhibits. That is why I should like to observe that certain segments for the Defence of Miroslav Tadic will also be presented in a part of the Defence case for Simo Zaric, and I will be quite frank that we will be most interested in the place and role of Miroslav Tadic in the 4th Detachment, as we have been able to see from the list of witnesses and exhibits proposed by the Defence counsel for Mr. Zaric. I should now like to go into concrete facts which we intend to prove in our case. With regard to the political involvement and participation of Miroslav Tadic in the institutions of authority prior to the war, it is the submission of the Defence that in the course of the Prosecution case, as well as in the Defence case for Dr. Simic, it has been proven that Miroslav Tadic had no involvement whatsoever in the political life in the municipalities of Samac and Odzak prior to the outbreak of the war. Without wishing to link anybody's political involvement or non-involvement to possible charges, unlike the Prosecution, we wish to underline and to support with evidence why Miroslav Tadic was appointed to the position of commander of the civil defence staff, a member of the Crisis Staff, and why he held a position in the 4th Detachment, and finally, why he was a member of the Exchange Commission. The Defence will seek to prove that Miroslav Tadic, throughout his activities during the indictment period, worked exclusively in the interest of all the citizens of Samac. We shall seek to prove that he was appointed to the 4th Detachment and to the civil defence in view of his professional experience, familiarity with the inhabitants and circumstances in Samac, and that he joined in the exchange processes after Serbs were detained in Odzak municipality for those same reasons, because he knew the people involved and because he was a respected citizen, a responsible and conscientious negotiator that everyone trusted. During his activities in the Crisis Staff, Miroslav Tadic relied in his work exclusively on legal obligations and provisions which determined his function as commander of the civil defence staff, and not by any political positions, instructions, or convictions. In addition to this fact, the Defence submits that his overall work in civil defence and exchange procedures was based on those same principles. His attitude primarily towards people, both those he knew and did not know but whom he encountered in the course of his duties, will be a separate segment of our case. The Defence will seek to prove that during his work and general conduct outside his professional duties, Tadic was never encumbered by any kind of political convictions, least of all by any kind of intolerance towards any individual or any ethnic group. Miroslav Tadic was a member of the 4th Detachment. He was mobilised, as were the other citizens of Samac who responded to the mobilisation of the state which they recognised and which they considered their own, and by the competent officers of the Yugoslav People's Army, he was appointed to the position of assistant commander for logistics. The Defence submits that Tadic's appointment to this post was motivated exclusively by the good reputation he had acquired, both as a teacher and as a successful caterer, and also in view of his age. This lifelong experience, his knowledge of people and his popularity, I would be free to say, as a caterer, were closely related to the position he held in that detachment. We will go on to prove that apart from this formal appointment to the position of assistant commander for logistics, Tadic never really performed those duties, nor did he assume any obligation stemming from that function in any form. Therefore, he neither committed, nor ordered, nor aided and abetted third parties in this. In the course of its defence case, the Defence will prove that the headquarters of the 4th Detachment were never located in the coffee bar AS. It doesn't need a great deal of common sense and logic to come to the conclusion that it is quite natural for people working in a particular institution to gather in a coffee bar nearby. Members of the 4th Detachment did visit the AS cafe while the command was in the SIT premises, and even later, when the SIT building was used as a barracks, and up to this present day, when the barracks moved out, the officers and soldiers would come to the coffee bar, wearing uniform and in civilian clothes. I would see them there too, because I would often go there and visit my client when he was on provisional release. The barracks was in the SIT premises and they were sitting in the AS cafe. The Defence believes that even now, when the workers have gone into SIT premises once again to start doing their normal duties and working there, they will continue to come to the AS cafe. In addition to the evidence already presented through the testimony of witnesses who were daily guests of this coffee bar and members of all ethnic groups, who had nothing to do with the 4th Detachment, nor any other military or political institution, God forbid, or any paramilitary institution, God forbid, will provide evidence on the work of this coffee bar. With respect to this fact, the Defence will present evidence which, unlike the Prosecution, are not hearsay evidence but direct evidence of authentic eyewitnesses who have direct knowledge about all these things. The Defence will provide evidence to prove when Miroslav Tadic became a member of the Crisis Staff and until when he was a member of that institution. We believe that we have already clearly articulated the position of the Defence regarding this in the course of the Prosecution case, as well as during the Defence case of Mr. Simic. This essential fact, in our view, is something we wish to highlight in particular because we feel that the indictment is very vague in that regard. Namely, the Prosecutor herself, in paragraph 2 of the indictment, determines very vaguely the period of membership of Miroslav Tadic in the Crisis Staff. Allow me to remind you what the Prosecutor says in paragraph 2 of the indictment. "After the 17th of April, 1992, Miroslav Tadic became chairman of the Bosanski Samac Exchange Commission and was responsible for organising and carrying out the majority of so-called prisoner "exchanges" through which non-Serb civilians were expelled from their homes." The next witness for me is extremely important, and I think I already referred to it in my motion for acquittal. He remained a member of the Exchange Commission until at least 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I didn't want to interrupt my colleague. But here it says the next witness for me is extremely important. Next paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises. A slip of the tongue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next witness certainly is important for me but I said something else. The next sentence is important me. He remained a member of the Exchange Commission until at least 1995, while serving in the capacity of chairman of the Exchange Commission, Miroslav Tadic also was a member of the Crisis Staff. That is what the Prosecutor says. In the motion for acquittal pursuant to Rule 98 of the Rules of Procedure, the Defence felt that an undefined time period linked to the functions performed by my client was an encumbrance for or a disadvantage for the Defence. If the Prosecutor wished to link his function as a member of the Crisis Staff to his position as president of the Exchange Commission, then he at least should have been precise enough to say when Tadic was chairman of the Exchange Commission. If he links this to membership in the Exchange Commission, then it is up to the Tadic Defence to prove that the Crisis Staff did not exist up to 1995, when Tadic was still working, but only as an associate of the republic commission for exchange. The Prosecution, and I wish to remind the Trial Chamber of this, tendered Exhibit P83, that Tadic became a member of the Exchange Commission, and I underline the word "member" in October 1992, when the Crisis Staff no longer existed. That is why the Defence will seek to prove membership of Miroslav Tadic in the Crisis Staff through very clear testimony, supported by precise documents, without denying that while he was a member of the Crisis Staff, Tadic took an active part in the process of exchange. The Defence will prove that Tadic became a member of the Crisis Staff on the 23rd of April, 1992, that is, after the day he was appointed commander of the civil defence staff, and that he stayed in that position while the same existed, that is, up to July 1992. The Defence will also prove that Tadic was not a member of the War Presidency, nor did he have any position whatsoever in the assembly bodies as of January 1993, and also - and I think that is not in dispute in this case - that he was not a member of any assembly body after 1993 or before the war; he simply never was a member of any assembly body throughout his lifetime. Maybe it is now time for me to make a break, because I'm moving on to a new issue now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We will take our break and continue our proceedings at 1615 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was discussing the positions of the Defence regarding the place and role of Mr. Tadic in the Crisis Staff, so allow me to say a few more words about the position of the Defence and the way in which we intend to prove certain facts. First of all, I wish to say that in the understanding of the Defence, the Prosecutor believes that the position somebody had in the authorities was de jure and de facto, a clearly important factor in endeavours to prove that the activities of an accused are part of a common enterprise. The Defence does not wish to enter into a polemic with such theses of the Prosecutor at this stage, but is surprised that in the indictment, nor in the course of the Prosecution case, did the Prosecution inquire into the positions Tadic held within the system of authority as of the April events of 1992. The Defence is of the opinion that the Prosecution, ever since the indictment was issued and amended several times, even after my client was interviewed, intentionally neglected this function that he had. Unlike the Prosecution, the Defence submits that the evidence that it will present linked to this position will elucidate to a high degree the overall activities and conduct of Miroslav Tadic. That is why, in the presentation of evidence, the Defence will seek to prove that this function and position as commander of the civil defence staff is directly linked with his membership in the Crisis Staff and the system of authority and that it did not have anything to do or was in no way connected with any particular policies. This is a function that the Prosecution was not interested in in the least in the general allegations contained in the indictment. The appointment of Miroslav Tadic as commander of the civil defence staff, you have seen the exhibit - the date is the 23rd of April, 1992 - was the basis on which he joined the Crisis Staff. And in view of the fact that the very notion of the Crisis Staff, in the eyes of the Prosecution, is a reflection of negative policies, the Defence will devote special attention to this aspect of his work in its case, and I should like to make some indications of that in this opening statement. During the Defence case of Dr. Blagoje Simic, this Honourable Trial Chamber was able to familiarise itself with the concept of civil defence. You were tendered exhibits, such as the law on Defence. You probably remember D80/30, and the decree on civil defence, Exhibit D81/3, which we consider provide the legal frameworks, with some precision, of the place and role of the civil defence in the system of defence. It has already become undisputed, I hope, to this Trial Chamber that the shelling of Samac was frequent, shelling of a town full of civilian population, a town without any strategic military facilities. I would like to assert that that shelling occurred on a daily basis. And this was coupled with all kinds of problems, such as the shortage of food, commodities, electricity, water, disease, and refugees. The significance of this defence to remove the consequences and to normalise life became immeasurable. There was hardly one aspect of the tasks of the civil defence provided for by law that was not a real, visible, acute problem in Samac which the civil defence needed to address. The Defence will also seek to prove the conditions under which the work of that staff was organised at the beginning of the war. You will hear testimony that will describe that both Serbs and Muslims and Croats worked together in that staff, together and in harmony and with equal enthusiasm, that these were mostly elderly people, pensioners, without any kind of prejudices but guided by their personal wishes to assist, through their work, all the citizens of the Samac municipality. The Defence will seek to prove that the activity of that staff, this small group of people, made a very significant contribution to the normalisation of life in those difficult times and that all citizens of good intentions of Samac remember and mention the name of Miroslav Tadic in the context of those activities, describing him in the most favourable terms. The work on repairing damage caused by shelling, securing and protecting key civilian facilities, hospitals, health centres, post offices, the glazing of homes, the organisation of funerals, the building of coffins for burying the dead in the whole region, the provision of temporary accommodation for people rendered homeless by the shelling, the organisation of the evacuation of women and children to Serbia, are only one part of those activities, even though Miroslav Tadic himself had no authority over the work of the local Red Cross, through a number of testimonies, the Defence intends to throw light on the work of this institution, which also, without any prejudices, extended great assistance to all the citizens of Samac during the war and within its area contributed significantly to alleviating the suffering of the civilian population caused by the war operations. A number of written documents will be presented, and you will also hear live testimony on the work of this organisation, demonstrating unequivocally that members of all ethnic groups worked together and that they provided aid to all citizens, irrespective of their ethnicity. Humaneness as one of the basic principles of aid to the afflicted population at times of war, was both an instrument and a goal pursued both by the civil defence staff and the local Red Cross. If all these activities of the civil defence staff and its commander are elucidated, at least to some extent, the Defence is quite confident that this Honourable Trial Chamber will find it easy to establish the real truth, both with regard to the personality of Miroslav Tadic himself and with regard to his involvement in the work of the Crisis Staff and in the exchange procedures. Fully appreciative of the highly professional approach of this Trial Chamber to the establishment of all details of significance for establishing the real truth, the Defence emphasises that it is very important for the Chamber to familiarise itself in detail with the position of the civil defence in the system of defence and its competences. That is why even before the beginning of our case we have tendered both these fundamental regulations, the law on defence and the decree on civil defence, so we believe the Trial Chamber is familiar with these documents. We did not wish to analyse in detail with Mr. Ninkovic all the important items of these regulations, but I take advantage of this opening statement to underline that these documents clearly define the role of the civil defence, its relationship with other areas of defence, as well as with the authorities as such, and we believe that this Trial Chamber will note all these things with due attention while reading these documents. The Defence will set out to prove that Miroslav Tadic, neither as an individual nor as part of the duties he performed, had anything to do with what the Prosecutor describes as forced labour, and the Defence as work duty. It was a pure coincidence that the offices of the coordinator of work duty and the place where people rallied who went to perform work duty and the fact that they saw Tadic in that building where the offices of the civil defence and Red Cross staff were located, and this coincidence may have led uninformed people to come to the conclusion that Tadic had something to do with the organisation of activities under work duty. In the absence of other evidence, the Prosecution has tried to construe this as a fact, and we shall further analyse this in our final brief. Without wishing in any way to disassociate ourselves from work duty in saying this, the purpose of our defence is to present the place and role of the accused Mr. Tadic in objective and truthful terms. Miroslav Tadic, from the very first moment he came into contact with investigators of the Prosecution, up to his Initial Appearance in this Tribunal, never intended to belittle his role in the Samac events, but on the contrary, to present them truthfully. Our Defence team considers it to be our professional and moral duty to act along the same lines as our client with this regard. In that light, we will elucidate his positions linked to work duty. Unlike many other institutions which did use work duty services, to all people who came to the civil defence staff as part of their work duty, work in the civil defence was an advantage. They wanted to continue working there and to avoid being transferred by the coordinators to some other activities, even though in the civil defence too there were some very difficult and unpleasant duties, which you will hear about through the testimony of people who carried them out. You will also hear from them that good interpersonal relations, based on confidence, comradeship, aid, regardless of ethnic affiliation, among the workers of that staff were the basis on which that staff acted. Witnesses will confirm that a positive attitude and atmosphere that governed the work of that staff was, to a great deal, the merit of this person, who is now the accused Miroslav Tadic Brko, who was always known as the Mustasio because of his moustache. The Defence will also set out to prove that Miroslav Tadic has nothing to do with other things that he is being charged with under item 14C of the indictment. Cruel and inhumane treatment of Bosnian Croats and Bosnian Muslims and other non-Serb civilians, including beatings, torture, forced labour assignments, and confinement under inhumane conditions. I wish to emphasise in particular that with respect to these charges, the Prosecutor, in his written response to the motion for acquittal relating to Article 98 bis, did not stipulate a single word or mention a single piece of evidence against my client. When the Prosecutor cannot find a single piece of evidence necessary to satisfy the standards required according to Article 98 bis, why then should it be incumbent upon the Defence to interpret the Prosecution's evidence and to offer its own and to emphasise the goal of the defence procedure? However, it is the duty of the Defence team, as the charges and counts in the indictment exist, to provide relevant evidence and proof, and it will do so, and it will prevail upon the Trial Chamber and show that Tadic, without any doubt, had nothing to do with the charges and counts contained in the indictment against him. In relation to the plunder and looting of property from paragraph 14 of the indictment, the Defence will provide firm and unequivocal evidence which will serve to acquit our client. The Prosecutor has no serious proof or evidence to prove these charges. The Prosecutor claims in his response to the request following Article 98, in paragraph 44, that this action is incorporated within the notion of forced labour, and then makes no mention of anything else with respect to looting and plunder. We shall deal with this thesis in our closing argument, but I should just like to underline that this thing that has been construed by the Prosecution will be refuted through our arguments, and that is that Miroslav Tadic had nothing to do with issuing forced labour assignments. The next point that I wish to make in my opening statement has to do with exchanges. The word used in the indictment and in the Prosecution case, which is most linked to the name and conduct of my client, the word "exchange" which the Prosecutor, in paragraph 2, uses inverted commas for and refers to so-called prisoner exchanges, explains to the Court that it was through these exchanges that non-Serbs were expelled from their homes. The word and concept for which the members of this Honourable Trial Chamber asked a number of questions, both of the Prosecution and of witnesses, and even of the Defence team itself, seeking clarification and explanation of the concept of exchange, as well as the procedure under which these exchanges took place. I believe, Your Honours, that you have already gained an insight into all these matters, and it is our professional and human task to prove to you what the Prosecutor has not succeeded in doing, and that is the basic question: What the goal of the exchanges was. Your Honours, I should like to mention at this juncture that I needed very many days, even months, to put all the pieces of the jigsaw puzzle together and give you a picture of the exchanges themselves. I had to understand all the essential factors in this complicated procedure, to which there were always two sides, two parties. There was always the request made by one side, the goodwill of the other side, but this was always limited by certain terms and circumstances of an agreement, the desire expressed by the subjects themselves to be exchanged, the limited possibilities to take in those persons on their own territory, and the Defence will present evidence on all these important matters. But why exchanges at all? In whose interest were they conducted? What were the motives for those working in matters of exchange? When you come to hear the witnesses in these proceedings, when you have read the written evidence, you will arrive at only one possible conclusion. I'm not going to impose that conclusion upon you, but I will say that we shall seek to prove that the exchanges were not at all for curtailing any human rights, but rather that they were a means of realising human rights themselves. In light of this standard and position, the Defence will provide a series of evidence and proof. You will first of all hear that the exchanges are no brain child of Miroslav Tadic or the town of Samac itself either. You have already heard that even before April 1992, on the territory of the Samac municipality, exchanges took place between Croatia and Yugoslavia. You will hear that the exchanges took place in a spontaneous way in other places in the Posavina region as well. You will also hear the types of people that were engaged and involved in this process of exchanges. You will also be able to see that these were things that were done by professors. They included teachers, social workers, lawyers, judges, all manner of persons. You will also hear that it was a process that was implemented throughout the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that commissions were set up, also at government level, at the level of the BH government, the Federation, the Muslim one, and the Croatian side, the HVO, as well, and also finally on the Serb side too; that those commissions were organised at the level of the municipalities, regions, and republics; that there were military and civilian segments in those commissions. The Prosecution and the Defence agreed that you should be presented evidence according to which the exchanges took place in a very similar fashion, almost identically in the Posavina region and throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina and even in the territory of the whole of the former Yugoslavia. But quite obviously, we are dealing with different motives, why presentation of evidence has been made in this way to the Trial Chamber. Let me remind you that most of the documents that the Prosecution provided were contained in document P146. The position of the Prosecution that this was an image of widespread and systematic plan of attack on the civilian population is something that the Defence will be analysing in its closing arguments, but all we're going to do now is ask the question of where this kind of logics can lead the Prosecution. Are we going to follow up that thesis here or in some other dock, bring to trial hundreds of members of Serb, Muslim, Croatian military and civilian commission? That is the question. Are we going to be obliged to bring in as witnesses thousands of people from all over the territory of the former Yugoslavia to tell us here before us and you of the kind of gratitude and admiration they have towards these people who wanted to reduce their sufferings and do whatever they could to help them escape from a very difficult way of life? To fulfil their wishes, to allow these people, at least for a moment, to believe in better days, days which they envisage by this imaginary but very real separation line, and crossing it. Do I have to remind you of the words uttered by Prosecution witnesses in explaining the joy they felt when they heard that they would be up for an exchange? And some of them even said that that was the best day of their lives, when they heard the news. That is why without wishing in any way to sound pathetic, I would like to say that through the Defence of Miroslav Tadic and his work in the exchange process, we shall be defending the whole principle of exchange, and all the people who worked honestly and we believe humanely in this very difficult task throughout the war years. You will hear, and we shall present to you, documents which testify to the fact that the exchanges were discussed and decided upon by the negotiators of all three entities at the highest level within the frameworks of frequent peace negotiations. You will also hear that the exchanges of both military and civilian persons, significant decisions were made and declarations, stemming from the Geneva negotiations and negotiations in Budapest between the two wars parties on the territory of the former Yugoslavia, ranging up to declarations of the International Red Cross and the officials of that organisation. And finally, you will also be in a position to hear that the exchanges themselves, both military and civilian, were the subject of a special section of the Dayton Accords themselves. We shall present to you a significant number of documents which, along with the authentic testimony of witnesses, will clearly and unequivocally show the entire hierarchy of decision making on the subject of exchanges, without the need for any explanation, you will be able to see who was asked about the exchanges. You will see whether an individual was allowed to go for an exchange or not, both in the civilian and military structures. You will be able to see how the decision-making was made, both on the Serb side, the Croatian side, and the Muslim commissions as well. I should like here and now, precisely because we're talking about the exchanges, to deal with one more subject which the Defence would like to bring before this Tribunal and Court, and comes up against a wall of argument with the tu quoque presentations. Your Honours, the Defence fully respects the position of this Trial Chamber and positive humanitarian law on the -- on prescribing discussions of what others did and justifying one crime by the fact that other crimes were committed. This principle is quite clear to us and unequivocal from the practice so far in the Tribunal.
