But these rigid legal formalisms which lead to a priori rejection of the probability of listening to testimony about some other events and referring to this principle alone will not, in our humble opinion, lead you to that ultimate goal, the goal of truth, but will leave you in the realm of conjecture and surmise as to some vital facts. It is precisely these exchanges, the concept of the changes, their goals and consequence, that incorporate two subjects at the very least, two parties which are in conflict and they relate to different destinies, and they relate to people on both the two warring sides. It is not our aim, Your Honours, in these proceedings in any way to bring to light the actions, let me be quite blunt, the crimes of the opposite side. We shall respect and abide by every ruling on the part of the Trial Chamber if we overstep our limits and what is relevant for these proceedings. But I have to mention on this occasion that you will not be able to gain complete insight and understanding of any of the conduct of the participants in the exchange, including my client, unless you hear who was exchanged, what the people being exchanged desired, what the relationship was between the people coming up for an exchange towards those people that brought them in for the exchange, regardless of what side they came from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic. On that topic of whether or not we need to hear the whole scenario of exchanges, the Trial Chamber, as you have rightly pointed, has a stand on evidence that appears to bring in the tu quoque issue. As long as the explanation is only limited to offering the defence for Mr. Miroslav Tadic or the evidence is allowed to that extent, then you will be allowed to bring in that evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am very happy to hear the position of the Trial Chamber, because I would like to say that mens rea, and motive as well, in all these crimes is a very vital element that ought to be elucidated before this Trial Chamber, and that is why I mentioned the facts I did. In the aim of clarifying the exchange procedure fully, and especially in refuting the thesis of the Prosecution in the indictment that the exchanges were veiled ethnic cleansing, as well as the role of Miroslav Tadic in those exchanges, the Defence has prepared a series of evidence. You will hear testimony from several witnesses who took an active part in the work of different commissions for exchanges, both civilian and military and the commissions of the opposite sides. They will all be testifying viva voce about their work, about their cooperation with my client, about their direct knowledge as eyewitnesses, about the conduct and behaviour of Miroslav Tadic in those very difficult and sensitive affairs, affairs in which, even in the smallest gesture, you will see the subjective relationship of one man towards his fellows and in which humaneness and self-commitment is proved and demonstrated. You will hear individual stories, brief recollections of the events which, according to the understanding of the Defence, reflected the humaneness in the personality of my client, and this needs no explanation but speaks for itself. It speaks about the man Miroslav Tadic, in the same way that he was described by Witness Q in this very courtroom here and when he explained why he said what he did about him. You will hear viva voce from the testimony of persons the Prosecution did not see as being victims, persons of non-Serb ethnicity who were called up in the exchanges but who wished to remain in Samac. These were persons whom nobody forced, either directly or indirectly, to leave their own hometown. These were persons who also woke up on the 17th of April, 1992, in their own homes, just like the Prosecution witnesses in this trial, in their own native town, and on that particular morning they did not wish to leave Samac, and they never did leave it. And you will hear what these people think about the conduct and behaviour of Miroslav Tadic and his involvement in the exchanges. You will have depositions and you will have statements according to Rule 92 bis, and you will -- they will provide you with an opportunity to learn about what people from Batkovici have to say who went for the exchange and used the right of choice, whether they wished to be exchanged or not, whether they wished to stay in their own homes, and what their decisions were, and where they are now. Then you will also hear from people from Samac who were invited by the commissions of the opposite sides to be exchanged but who refused this offer and stated their views. It is these small threads in the broad weave of human destinies that we shall endeavour to elucidate in this trial, the role and place of our client in the exchanges, but not as a mask and veil for ethnic cleansing, of course, but as a humane act in helping these people escape from the war and in reuniting families whose members had been separated. I should just like to add at this point that the Defence, during the Prosecution case, Miroslav Tadic's Defence, took note of the procedure before the military courts that was brought up, and it was in our interest that through the Prosecution witnesses in this area under investigation first of all to arrive at proof and evidence which will support the role of the military courts in Batkovici in view of the positions of Miroslav Tadic in the exchanges and the possibility of his alleged decisions on the exchanges. We have seen that the Trial Chamber has shown a certain amount of interest for these proceedings, although we feel not only that Miroslav Tadic but any of the clients sitting here has anything to do with these military court proceedings. And in view of the interest shown by the Trial Chamber, we have prepared certain evidence, in fact witnesses, who were active participants and defence lawyers in those trials to explain the procedure and what was done in each individual case. With respect to proving the facts concerning the exchanges, the Defence also has two video recordings to show about the negotiations and the exchanges themselves. One of the tapes is the exchange between the Serb and Muslim side which took place in May 1993, and the second video recording is the exchange from Dragalic, and a lot has been said about that in this court, and it dates to June 1993, that particular exchange. And the Defence feels that this Trial Chamber, by having an insight into this material, especially with respect to the negotiations, because in the -- Prosecution only showed the procedure itself. But we are going to focus on the negotiations. And the Trial Chamber will gain a complete picture of how the negotiations were conducted themselves, the participation of my client in those negotiations, and the exchange process itself. For this opening statement, we have prepared two and a half minutes of those tape recordings, with the aim of giving the Trial Chamber visual insight into the area surrounding the petrol pump in Dragalic, which was mentioned a number of times in this courtroom and which will be mentioned many more times again in the Defence case. This will give you an overview of the surroundings preceding the negotiations, the surroundings and conditions in which the negotiations took place, which we feel is a very important aspect of the process of exchange. There is no comment accompanying the videotapes. I think that the images will be sufficient, and I now call upon the technical booth to play the tapes, and we'll be discussing them a great deal during the Defence case itself. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall go back to those video recordings. I think that they are very useful in order to give the Trial Chamber an insight into what took place. You will see one of the Prosecution witnesses himself, who spoke about those exchanges, and the Defence feels that this is interesting material. The Defence will seek to prove just how incorrect and untruthful -- yes, let me be blunt and say sometimes deliberately a false portrayal of the conduct of my client through certain witness testimonies on the part of Prosecution witnesses. The Defence will place the real facts before the Trial Chamber, eyewitnesses to the conduct of Miroslav Tadic in a series of episodes that were presented during the Prosecution case and the presentation of its evidence. In that way, you will hear where he was, what he did, and how he behaved, how Miroslav Tadic behaved in those first days of the war. You will hear witness testimony about his presence and conduct when the weapons were handed over and when certain individuals were detained in the first days of the war. The Prosecution, on several occasions, attempted to present evidence on the alleged extortion of money on the part of Miroslav Tadic. These assertions on the part of the Prosecution, regardless whether directly or indirectly, can be incorporated into the actus rea of the charges, and they had an influence on the presentation of evidence by the Defence. It is our wish to throw light on the personality of Miroslav Tadic from all the angles where it was tainted by the Prosecution and that these should not remain within the frameworks of the standard of proof that is necessary for reasonable -- to go beyond reasonable doubt. The Defence will provide proof which unequivocally meet these standards of complete material truth. The Defence will seek to prove that Miroslav Tadic never asked anybody or received any kind of unlawful remuneration for his work and that the stories told by well-intentioned people gave rise to the wrong conclusions and with malicious people they distorted the truth and were tendentious. The Defence will also seek to prove that what the Prosecution construed was completely groundless, that Tadic, in allegedly taking money, was the person who decided who could and could not be exchanged. The Defence considers that the thesis placed by the Prosecution in its response to the motion for acquittal is even less groundless [sic] and which stems from the thesis that Tadic enforced persecution through unlawful arrest and detention of persons. The Defence will therefore clearly and unequivocally seek to prove that Miroslav Tadic did not have anything to do whatsoever with anybody's arrest and detention, regardless of whether those arrests and detentions were considered to be lawful or unlawful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting you, but on page 52 - let me see now - some mistake. It's line 22, yes, indeed, where it reads, beginning from line 21: "The Defence considers that the thesis placed by the Prosecution in its response to the motion for acquittal is even --" it should be more groundless instead of less groundless, I guess, because otherwise it doesn't make sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter misspoke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]. Yes, that it is groundless, in fact. I agree. I can repeat, but I think that it is clear now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: No, no. It is clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the Defence considers that Miroslav Tadic had nothing to do with anybody's arrest or detention. The Defence would like to say a few more words about another aspect and area, and I'm drawing to the close of my opening statement now. I'm talking about the population report, demographic expert report. Although this piece of evidence is a joint piece of evidence for all three Defence teams, I shall use the agreement of my colleagues to present certain introductory remarks to that expert report. It is the aim of our expert population report -- our aim is twofold, in fact. On the one hand, we wish to present to the Trial Chamber the conclusions that can be made from the sole true demographic sources, for it to be both scientific and professionally based, without any constructions or conjecture and surmise. On the other hand, we shall seek to prove during our Defence case that the methodology used by the Prosecution expert on population is completely scientifically unfounded and completely arbitrary. Although the assessment made by the Prosecution is contained in the closing argument, in expert opinions of this kind, it is necessary and indispensable, and these are highly professional areas for which all of us legal men have to invest special effort in order to be able to understand the matter and material in hand -- as I say, it is necessary to give clear-cut, scientific methodological analyses in the approach to the task in hand, the task set, because only in that way shall we be able to understand the method of work, that is to say, the expert opinion itself, and the final results of the work in hand, that is to say, the conclusions of the experts. In that sense, before this Trial Chamber we have the written report, and we'll probably be hearing orally from a leading Yugoslav expert for population matters, and her name is Dr. Svetlana Radovanovic. Her specialty for many years is not the death rate and the birth rate alone, but demographic changes in the structure of the population throughout the territory of the former Yugoslavia, with particular emphasis on collation of personal ID numbers and figures. This is something that the Prosecution expert witness explained to the Trial Chamber. Our own expert has a great deal of experience with the problem of collation of numbers, especially in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, and the problems with the personal identification numbers which this collation is performed in order to be able to draw any scientifically based professional conclusions which would be of assistance to this Trial Chamber. Depending on how far we have insight into the documents and how far the Prosecution had material from the statistical authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina and the OSCE, our own demographic expert will provide an integral and, might I say, completely argumentative expert opinion, the real kind, and the only kind that can be valid. In coming to the end of our opening statement, I should like to say that we do not know if we have met the goals set before us as a Defence team. This will become evident through the presentation of evidence and the continuation of the trial itself, the Defence case. We will be very happy if you seek clarification on any point from our witnesses. In this trial, the Defence has set itself a clear-cut goal. Once we have reached the end of these proceedings, by which time Miroslav Tadic will have spent a full four years in the Detention Unit, he will be told by this Honourable Trial Chamber what he has been expecting to hear all along, ever since he first learnt of the indictment against him. He will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, when you say that he has spent a full four years, it doesn't exclude the time when he was on provisional release?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Presiding Judge, Your Honour Judge Mumba, I said at the end, or perhaps I don't know how long the trial will last, but Miroslav Tadic surrendered to the Tribunal, as I said, in the beginning, in February 1998, and he was provisionally released for a period of one year and three or four months. In February this year it will be five full years since the time he gave himself up, minus that period of one year and several months. So that -- of course, we don't know when this trial will come to a close, but that's why I say that at the end of the trial this will be almost four years, in my own assessment. And my last sentence, if I may: I want to say that Miroslav Tadic will hear you, this Honourable Trial Chamber, pronounce him not guilty of the charges against him. That concludes my opening statement. May I make some technical remarks in closing? The Defence team of Mr. Miroslav Tadic, as you know, will have seven viva voce witnesses, one of them videolink witness, which will be heard when the Trial Chamber decides to hear him, and then the Trial Chamber asked for two more witnesses that were to have been heard through deposition. They will testify. This was something that the Trial Chamber asked. They asked for viva voce testimony, if you recall. For one of them I asked that he be heard on the basis of a deposition. But I think that in the first segment he will be present here in Court. We just have some technical problems. He hasn't got a passport at the moment, but we hope that we will be able to overcome these difficulties in the next few days. I'm talking about Dario Radic. So I hope that he will be able to come in for testimony. So it is the Defence plan that after we hear all these witnesses, irrespective of the videolinks, we hear Miroslav Tadic testify himself. My first witness is Mr. Velimir Maslic. I will be leading him. Would you like us to start? I have quite a number of documents that I have prepared for this witness. Would you like the witness to be shown in to court? I need five minutes to prepare myself, perhaps, but do you wish me to go ahead with the witness or shall we leave him for tomorrow? I'm at your disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The Trial Chamber feels that it's better to start with your witness tomorrow, when we start our proceedings, at 1415 in the afternoon. So you'll be -- you'll have enough time to prepare your documents so that the evidence will be flowing, without breaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Are there any other matters to be raised before we rise? I see none. We shall adjourn now and continue our proceedings tomorrow at 1415 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 16th day of January 2003, at 2.15 p.m. 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 5.15 p.m.,
